analysis.one_liner: Freezes new federal rulemaking and suspends recently issued regulations until Congress passes cost-benefit reform.
analysis.headline: The House passed a freeze on new federal regulations 276-146, but the Senate never voted on it, and no moratorium ever took effect.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar every federal agency from taking almost any step toward writing new regulations — from early notices to final rules — from late 1994 until the end of 1995, or until Congress enacted a law requiring cost-benefit and risk analysis of rules. It would also suspend rules issued in the meantime, and it would extend a separate freeze on Endangered Species Act listings into 1996. Emergency threats to health or safety, criminal law enforcement, and civil rights rules were carved out, as were favored items like telecom spectrum auctions and textile import rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing pending regulations — manufacturers, chemical plants, land developers, food processors — would gain time free of new federal rules, and rules issued since November 1994 would be suspended. Small businesses with 100 or fewer employees would get six more months beyond that before suspended rules applied to them. Companies in explicitly favored sectors, like wireless licensees and textile importers, would be exempted entirely.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars federal agencies from any rulemaking step — including notices of proposed rulemaking — from November 20, 1994 until the earlier of December 31, 1995 or enactment of laws requiring cost-benefit analysis and standardized risk assessment for federal rules.
It suspends the effectiveness of any rule issued or made effective during that window, starting 30 days after enactment, unless a waiver is granted.
It postpones any statutory, regulatory, or court-ordered deadline tied to frozen rulemaking by five months or until the moratorium ends.
It imposes a special, longer moratorium on listing endangered or threatened species and designating critical habitat, running until the end of 1996 or the enactment of Endangered Species Act funding.

Actions limited to repealing or streamlining existing rules are excluded if the agency head and the OMB regulatory administrator certify them in writing, so agencies could keep deregulating but not regulate.

analysis.who_pays: People waiting on rules that protect their health, safety, workplaces, and environment — worker-safety, consumer, environmental, and other rules in progress would be frozen, and rules issued after November 1994 would be suspended. Communities affected by suspended rules and delayed endangered-species listings bear the risk. Waivers are available for imminent threats to health or safety, criminal law enforcement, and civil rights rules, but each waiver requires sign-off by the OMB regulatory administrator.
analysis.who_pays_short: People awaiting health, safety, and environmental rules

drawbacks.text: The moratorium is one-directional: agencies could keep repealing or narrowing existing rules with a written certification, but could not move any new protective rule forward, even a proposed one.

Exceptions are narrow and discretionary: an agency head must get a written waiver finding from the OMB regulatory administrator for each imminent health or safety threat, and the civil rights exception excludes any rulemaking that relies on quotas or preferences.
The bill bars anyone from suing a federal agency to enforce the moratorium's limits, so the only check is political.

Supporters' own stated goal was to force Congress to enact cost-benefit and risk-analysis requirements by freezing everything until it did — meaning new protections for workers, consumers, and the environment would be held hostage to separate legislation that might never pass.

The bill singles out favored exemptions — telecom spectrum auctions, textile import releases, sanctions against China over intellectual property, and stock exchange competition rules — which its supporters would have to defend as more urgent than health or safety rules, which still needed a waiver.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued that a brief freeze would give Congress time to pass process reforms making future rules weigh costs and benefits. But the bill goes far beyond a pause: it suspends rules already issued, extends a species-listing freeze into 1996, delays deadlines even when courts ordered them, exempts deregulatory actions while blocking new rules, and leaves enforcement to politics rather than courts. The benefit to regulated businesses of delayed compliance is concrete; the benefit to the public is indirect and dependent on separate legislation that is not part of this bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 276-146 on February 24, 1995, but the Senate referred it to its Governmental Affairs Committee and never acted, so it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom DeLay introduced the bill on January 9, 1995, and 145 members — 123 Republicans and 22 Democrats — cosponsored it.
The House Government Reform and Oversight Committee reported the bill amended by a 28-13 vote on February 13, 1995, after subcommittee hearings and markup.
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions failed 172-250, with 168 of 204 Democrats in favor and 224 of 229 Republicans against.
The House passed the bill 276-146: 225 of 230 Republicans and 51 of 204 Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill on February 27, 1995, referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs, and no further action was ever recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead in the narrow sense that no rules were suspended and the moratorium never took effect; regulated industries never got the statutory freeze they sought, and neither did Congress enact the cost-benefit reform law the moratorium was designed to force.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated industries didn't get the freeze

industries.industry: Regulated industries broadly (manufacturers, chemical, energy, land development)
industries.note: The bill freezes new rules and suspends rules issued since late 1994, delaying worker-safety, environmental, and consumer protections these businesses would otherwise face. The public bears the cost of that delay in the form of rules that arrive later or not at all.

The bill carves out a special, longer moratorium on listing endangered or threatened species and designating critical habitat, lasting into 1996. Protections for at-risk species would be stalled even after the general moratorium ended.

Any rule suspended by the moratorium would not apply to small businesses until six months after the moratorium ends, giving them a longer compliance holiday. Small businesses would also benefit from the broader freeze on new rules.
The bill explicitly exempts FCC spectrum-transfer and wireless licensing actions from the moratorium, so auctions and license awards would proceed on schedule while other rulemaking is frozen.

The bill exempts a rule allowing conditional release of textile imports suspected of violating U.S. quotas, along with related textile rulemaking, so import enforcement would be loosened while the rest of rulemaking is frozen.
